spans.content: Anisotropic Exciton Transport in Layered Hybrid
Perovskite Quantum Wells
Maria L. Okafor, Jun-ho Park, and Elena V. Rossi
Department of Physics, Northgate University, Northgate 40117
Institute for Functional Materials, Lakeshore Polytechnic, Lakeshore 90210
We report time-resolved photoluminescence microscopy of exciton transport in layered hybrid perovskite quantum
wells with butylammonium and hexylammonium spacer cations. By fitting the spatiotemporal evolution of the
emission profile with an anisotropic diffusion model that includes exciton-exciton annihilation, we extract
both the in-plane and the out-of-plane components of the diffusion tensor on the same sample. The in-plane
diffusivity exceeds the out-of-plane one by more than an order of magnitude and decreases systematically as the
organic spacer becomes longer. Our results identify the barrier thickness as the dominant control parameter for
interlayer exciton hopping and provide quantitative input for the design of layered optoelectronic devices.
Keywords: exciton diffusion; layered perovskites; quantum wells; time-resolved microscopy; anisotropy
1. Introduction
Layered hybrid perovskites have emerged as a
versatile platform for studying excitonic physics in
two dimensions, combining large binding energies with
strong light-matter coupling [1, 2]. In these
materials the inorganic lead-halide sheets act as
quantum wells, while the organic spacer cations form
insulating barriers that confine carriers to a few
atomic layers. The resulting exciton binding energy,
typically
E_{b}\approx200\,\mathrm{meV}
, exceeds the thermal
energy at room temperature by almost an order of
magnitude.
Despite this progress, the transport of excitons
across and along the layers remains poorly understood.
In-plane diffusion is usually described by a single
coefficient
D
, yet the structural anisotropy of the
lattice suggests that the diffusion tensor should have
distinct components
D_{\parallel}
and
D_{\perp}
. Direct
measurements of both components on the same sample are
scarce, because the out-of-plane channel is difficult
to access optically and is easily masked by
exciton-exciton annihilation at high excitation
density [3].
1.1 Scope of this work
In this work we combine time-resolved
photoluminescence microscopy with a rate-equation
model to extract the full diffusion tensor of a series
of

quantum wells. We show that the
in-plane diffusivity is roughly an order of magnitude
larger than the out-of-plane one, and that the ratio
depends systematically on the spacer length.
2. Methods
2.1 Sample preparation
Single crystals of the
compounds were grown by
slow cooling of a saturated hydroiodic acid solution
and exfoliated onto fused silica substrates in a
nitrogen glovebox. Flake thicknesses between
and
200\,\mathrm{nm}
were verified by atomic force microscopy,
and all samples were encapsulated with a thin polymer
layer before being transferred to the cryostat.
The optical response of each flake was characterized
by reflectance and photoluminescence spectroscopy at
10 K. For all samples the lowest exciton resonance
appears as a narrow line with a full width at half
maximum below 12 meV, and no emission from
lower-dimensional impurity phases was detected within
the sensitivity of the measurement.
The spatiotemporal exciton density
n(\mathbf{r},t)
is
described by the anisotropic rate equation
\frac{\partial n}{\partial t}=D_{\parallel}\nabla_{\parallel}^{2}n+D_{\perp}\frac{\partial^{2}n}{\partial z^{2}}-\gamma n-\Gamma n^{2}\tag{1}
where
\gamma
is the monomolecular decay rate and
\Gamma
the exciton-exciton annihilation coefficient.
The first two terms on the right-hand side describe
diffusion along the layers and across the barriers,
respectively. Equation (1) is solved numerically on a
cylindrical grid, and the result is convolved with the
instrument response before it is compared to the data.

2.2 Optical setup

120 fs duration and collected through an objective
with a numerical aperture of 0.9. The emission was
imaged onto a streak camera, which gives a temporal

\tau_{r}\approx5\,\mathrm{ps}
and a spatial
resolution of 0.4 µm in the focal plane.

2.5 Control experiments
To exclude artifacts from photodegradation, the
emission intensity at the excitation position was
monitored before and after every scan. Data sets in
which the intensity dropped by more than 5 percent
were discarded, which affected fewer than one in ten
scans.
In addition, a reference flake of the

was measured at the beginning and at the end of each
measurement day. The extracted

agreed
within the quoted uncertainty over the entire
campaign, confirming the long-term stability of the

3. Results and Discussion
3.1 In-plane diffusion
Figure 2 shows the mean-square displacement of the
emission profile as a function of delay time for the
three samples. At early times the profile broadens
linearly, consistent with normal diffusion, and the
slope yields an in-plane coefficient between 0.38 and
0.57 cm² s⁻¹. The values are about a factor of two
larger than those reported for thick polycrystalline
films [6], which we attribute to the absence of grain
boundaries in our exfoliated flakes.
At later times the broadening slows down and
eventually saturates. This behavior reflects the decay
of the exciton population on a time scale
\tau=1/\gamma\approx2.1\,\mathrm{ns}
rather than a change of
the transport regime, as confirmed by the fact that
the saturation value scales with the square root of
the effective lifetime.
The annihilation coefficient extracted from the
fluence series is
for the
samples, in good agreement with earlier estimates [7].
It is nearly independent of the spacer length.
A second source of uncertainty is the finite size of
the excitation spot, which has a full width at half
maximum of 0.8 µm. Because the profile is deconvolved
explicitly, the effect on the fitted diffusion
coefficients is below 3 percent for all samples.
We also checked whether heating by the pulse train
alters the transport. Lowering the repetition rate
from 5 MHz to 0.5 MHz changed the extracted
D_{\parallel}
by less than 4 percent, which rules out a significant
thermal contribution.
Taken together, these checks indicate that the
in-plane values reported in Table 1 are not limited by
experimental artifacts, so that the remaining
differences between samples can be attributed to the
structure of the quantum wells.

rather than a change of
the transport regime, as confirmed by the fact that
the saturation value scales with the square root of

3.2 Out-of-plane transport
The out-of-plane component is obtained from the
delayed emission that originates from layers adjacent
to the excited one. Because the emission profile along
the stacking direction cannot be resolved directly, we
infer
D_{\perp}
from the lateral amplitude of the signal
at long delay times, where interlayer hopping and
annihilation compete.
The extracted values range from
to
and fall below the in-plane
ones by a factor of 12 to 20. Longer spacer cations
reduce
D_{\perp}
by roughly 40 percent per added
methylene pair, which is compatible with a tunneling
picture in which the hopping rate decays exponentially
with the barrier thickness.
A weaker dependence on the spacer length is found
for the in-plane coefficient, which varies by less
than 10 percent over the series. We conclude that the
lateral transport is governed by the inorganic sheet,
whereas the vertical transport is controlled by the
organic barrier.
4. Conclusions
We have measured the full diffusion tensor of
exciton transport in layered hybrid perovskite quantum
wells by combining time-resolved microscopy with an
anisotropic rate-equation model. The in-plane
diffusivity is more than an order of magnitude larger
than the out-of-plane one, and only the latter depends
strongly on the length of the organic spacer.
These findings suggest that thin barriers should be
favored in devices that rely on vertical charge
extraction, whereas thick barriers can be used to
confine excitons within a single layer. Future work
should address the temperature dependence of both
coefficients and the role of dark excitons in the
interlayer channel.
